items.blurb: On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to investigate the planet's missing water. Here's why it mattered.

items.title: Torrential rain causes widespread flooding in South Florida
items.blurb: Entire neighbourhoods remain under water as disruptions impact schools, roads, hospitals and airports.

items.title: The Simons Observatory is Online and Surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background
items.blurb: The Simons Observatory is online and surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) in greater detail than ever before. It's looking for tiny fluctuations in the CMB caused by primordial gravitational waves. These waves, if detected, would be as close to slam-dunk evidence for the Big Bang that we can expect to find.

items.title: Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why
items.blurb: The answer to one of Earth's greatest geological mysteries may lie deep beneath our feet.

items.title: Ancient minerals reveal a missing chapter in Türkiye's mountain-building history
items.blurb: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25 million years ago, earlier than previously believed.

items.title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks
items.blurb: Solid–liquid mixing, where particles are dispersed in a liquid, is essential in many industrial processes such as slurry preparation, crystallization, precipitation, adsorption and dissolution. In such cases, effective mixing is critical for contact between particles and liquid, enabling mass transfer. Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define.

items.title: Researchers trace how gut microbes transform dietary plant sterols into circulating sulfated metabolites
items.blurb: Phytosterols are plant-derived compounds found in vegetable oils, nuts and seeds. They are studied for their ability to reduce cholesterol absorption, yet only about 5% enter the circulation and most are excreted. How gut bacteria influence their metabolism and tissue distribution has remained unclear.

items.title: Should we save every old building?
items.blurb: When you visit one of Norway's open-air museums, you can experience a piece of old Norway: log-built timber houses, farmsteads and farm complexes, often situated in a historic cultural landscape.

items.title: Turmeric supplements offer little benefit for knee osteoarthritis
items.blurb: A comprehensive review of clinical trials indicates that turmeric supplements had no meaningful effect on quality of life for people with knee osteoarthritis

items.title: First lunar-specific ground motion model could guide seismic hazard assessments on moon
items.blurb: Civil engineers looking forward to building structures on the moon need to know how ground motion from moonquakes will affect these buildings. But will ground motion models developed for Earth work well for the lunar landscape?

items.title: Watch: Sea level rise isn't just waves—how groundwater threatens coastal cities from below
items.blurb: With El Niño winter storms rolling in, coastal communities will naturally brace for the obvious: surging high tides, pounding waves and seawater spilling over seawalls. Decades of storm coverage have encouraged us to measure climate risk by what crashes onto the shoreline.

items.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
items.blurb: It's that time of year when Christmas ads start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

items.title: A 115 million‑year‑old 'algae rebellion' in Portugal's sea cliffs pushes back evolutionary timeline
items.blurb: Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropaleontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you're going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope.

items.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
items.blurb: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

items.title: Q&A: Schools that ban cellphones see uptick in test scores
items.blurb: We're nearing two milestones in the smartphone era. January will mark 20 years since Steve Jobs first unveiled the iPhone from a stage in San Francisco.

items.title: Reading the temperature fingerprints of electrocatalytic reactions
items.blurb: Electrocatalysis is key to turning renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals, and industrial electrolyzers typically operate at moderately elevated temperatures. Measuring how reaction rates change with temperature is also a powerful, yet underexplored, way to probe what controls them. Such measurements yield two quantities: an apparent activation enthalpy, reflecting the energetic cost of the reaction, and a prefactor, which is linked to the activation entropy.

items.title: Even AI thinks it's a man's job: Models reveal gender bias in resumes and hiring assessments
items.blurb: The first hurdle may arise even before an application is submitted. A woman asks artificial intelligence to help her write her resume: The system chooses words, highlights qualities and builds a profile. Then another system, perhaps based on the same model, evaluates that text. If both reproduce gender stereotypes, the risk is a double filter: Bias enters the application and is reinforced by the person selecting it.

items.title: Archaeology students find Roman treasures on first excavation
items.blurb: The discoveries include gold jewelry, inscriptions and a finely carved gemstone, and were made at a site in Redesdale, Northumberland.

items.title: Webb confirms first-of-its-kind merger of a supergiant and smaller sun-like star
items.blurb: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star on the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star Bao. Their discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.

items.title: Protecting wild bees in Europe through calcareous grassland management and connected habitats
items.blurb: Calcareous grasslands are wildflower-rich ecosystems that develop on shallow, alkaline, nutrient-poor soils over chalk or limestone bedrock. They are rare and important habitats for wild bees and other pollinators—yet how well they can support these valuable communities depends on how they are managed. An international research team, led by the University of Göttingen, has shown that long-term abandonment or intensive management threatens the diversity of wild bees. Extensive management of these areas, together with appropriate nature conservation measures in the surrounding landscape, is crucial. The findings were published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.

items.title: Who's to blame for a rogue AI? New legal framework maps accountability
items.blurb: Cyberattacks and other harms caused by artificial intelligence challenge the ability of laws to determine who is liable. Product liability law would point to the company that built the AI model, but AIs are trained on data the company didn't produce, and the legions of people who have used them also played a role. Free speech and social media immunity laws that treat an AI agent as responsible for its own actions could imply the AI agent deserves the same rights as a person.

items.title: Gen Z men more likely than boomers to hold traditional views
items.blurb: A report published today from the King's Global Institute for Women's Leadership has found that young men in Britain are more likely to misperceive society's views on gender compared to other generations. Researchers found that Gen Z males are more likely to think society holds traditional views about them and therefore may be conforming to social expectations most Britons have left behind.

items.title: Switching off cellular recycling gene increases yields of hard-to-make drug target proteins
items.blurb: With an unusual genetic modification that disabled cells' recycling systems, researchers found a way to make cells produce significantly larger amounts of the proteins used to discover and develop new medicines. The findings could help speed up drug development while reducing research and development costs.

items.title: One unusual tooth suggests Homo erectus shared southern China with another human species
items.blurb: One of the most important ancestors to humans was around for much longer than previously believed. That is the conclusion of a new international study published in Nature in which researchers, including scientists from the University of Copenhagen, analyzed nine fossil teeth discovered in two caves in southern China. The teeth are between 324,000 and 184,000 years old, extending the known timeline of Homo erectus by around 200,000 years.

items.title: Midsize mussels fared the worst during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome
items.blurb: During the record-breaking Pacific Northwest heat dome in 2021, a mussel's life depended on its size and location on the shoreline at Cattle Point on San Juan Island.

items.title: Shrinking ruthenium catalysts boosts ammonia production rate up to 57-fold
items.blurb: Ammonia is drawing renewed attention as a "magic container" for safely storing and transporting hydrogen, a promising clean energy source of the future, as well as a carbon-free fuel that does not emit greenhouse gases when burned. However, for ammonia to be widely used as a key fuel, improving the efficiency of its production process is essential.

items.title: Scalable photonic quantum computer provides new insights into the fundamentals that shape its performance
items.blurb: Photonics-based quantum computers open up new possibilities for investigating highly complex problems in mathematics and have the potential to revolutionize fields ranging from energy and chemical research to secure communications. By utilizing the unusual properties of light particles, they can perform calculations that pose enormous challenges even for the most powerful supercomputers—or remain entirely beyond their reach. At Paderborn University, researchers are now investigating a fundamental question using Germany's first scalable photonic quantum computer, a 'Gaussian boson sampler': which quantum resources are most important for the performance of these devices?

items.title: Tropical plantations reshape biodiversity in ways species counts alone cannot reveal
items.blurb: The conversion of tropical rainforests into intensively farmed rubber or oil palm plantations threatens global biodiversity. However, this does not necessarily lead to the increasing similarity of the remaining species in every case, as might be expected. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen discovered that organisms react very differently to intensive agriculture. The results are published in the journal Nature.

items.title: Newly described South China Sea crab suggests relatively recent shift from shallows to deeper waters
items.blurb: A newly described crab species from the South China Sea suggests a relatively recent shift in one crab lineage from intertidal habitats to deeper waters. Found at depths of about 100–300 meters (330–980 feet), Macromedaeus putrimanubriatus is closely related to the intertidal species M. orientalis.

items.title: Where in Europe could electric‑powered ferries create cleaner travel routes?
items.blurb: Electric battery-powered ferries use electricity from the shore to charge batteries on board. These batteries supply electric motors that propel the ship. On suitable routes, low-carbon electricity could make sea travel substantially cleaner and strengthen its potential as an alternative to flying.

items.title: Spectral clues suggest hollow-core magnetic jet in brightest-ever gamma-ray burst
items.blurb: A China–Italy joint research team has reconstructed the time-resolved spectrum of GRB 221009A, the brightest gamma-ray burst (GRB) ever observed, and proposed that the burst may have produced a magnetically dominated jet with a hollow core. This is presented as a possible interpretation of the emission line's rise-then-fall evolution rather than a direct detection.

items.title: Today's Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country
items.blurb: It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England's first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God's providence.

items.title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control
items.blurb: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.

items.title: Young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing during first year at sea
items.blurb: New research has revealed young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing in their epic first year at sea, strengthening the case for proposed new marine protected areas. The study was co-led by France's CNRS, the Center Scientifique de Monaco and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The international research team tracked 48 juvenile emperor penguins from three colonies around the Weddell Sea: Snow Hill Island, Jason Peninsula and Atka Bay.

items.title: Rac1-Abi-1 Signaling Links DNA Repair to Tumorigenesis
items.blurb: The DNA damage response governs genomic integrity, and abnormal DNA repair can drive tumorigenesis. We previously identified a Rac1-Abi-1 signaling pathway in which Rac1 activates protein phosphatase 5, leading to Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation and enhanced non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Given the error-prone nature of NHEJ and its potential to promote genomic instability, we sought to determine whether Rac1-Abi-1-mediated regulation of NHEJ contributes to tumorigenesis. Here, we demonstrate the tumorigenic role of Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation in nonmalignant cell models and multiple tumorigenesis models established using a newly generated genetically engineered Abi-1 mouse model. We first found that the dephospho-mimetic Abi-1-S323A mutant promoted transformation-associated phenotypes in nonmalignant human cells and enhanced orthotopic glioblastoma growth under unperturbed conditions. To further investigate its tumorigenic potential in vivo, we generated CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Abi-1-S296A knock-in mice, in which S296 corresponds to human S323. Abi-1-S296A mouse embryonic fibroblasts exhibited increased proliferation, while mutant mice developed spontaneous tumors involving lymphoid tissues and organs under unperturbed conditions. Furthermore, Abi-1-S296A increased susceptibility to tumorigenesis following DNA damage. In a low-dose whole-body irradiation model, Abi-1-S296A mice showed a trend toward shortened survival and increased tumor development, with lesions including Harderian gland papillary cystadenomas, round-cell neoplasms, and anaplastic sarcomas. In addition, in an azoxymethane/dextran sulfate sodium (AOM/DSS)-induced colorectal tumor model, Abi-1-S296A mice developed significantly more tumors and had a greater tumor burden. These findings identify Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation as a previously unrecognized regulator of tumorigenesis and establish a new mouse model for investigating the physiological and pathological consequences of constitutive activation of upstream NHEJ-regulatory signaling.

items.title: The Caenorhabditis elegans pangenome elucidates hyper-divergent region gene content to reveal extensive gene copy-number variation and a novel anthelmintic resistance locus
items.blurb: Caenorhabditis elegans has been a keystone model in biological research since the early 1970s, and it was the first metazoan to have its genome sequenced and assembled in 1998. Over the last few decades, the genetic and genomic resources developed for C. elegans made it one of the most powerful models for understanding metazoan biology. Recently, the C. elegans community has collected over 2,000 globally distributed wild strains, which after whole-genome sequencing, were found to contain punctuated regions of extreme genetic variation, called hyper-divergent regions (HDRs). HDRs have been described in organisms across the tree of life, including plants and humans, and genes in HDRs appear to be involved in adaptation, such as environmental response genes, parasitism genes, or immunity genes. However, the extreme genetic divergence at these loci complicates short-read alignments, and the genomic content of these regions in non-reference strains is largely uncharacterized. To define the gene content in HDRs, we de novo assembled and annotated genomes of 140 genetically diverse strains. These data enabled the construction of the first gene-based pangenome for the species. Among these strains, we characterized the landscape of structural variation and developed novel methods to quantify gene content diversity. We found that both variable copy-number and stable-copy environmental response genes were enriched in HDRs. These results further suggest that these regions have an important evolutionary role in adaptation to heterogeneous environments. We leveraged this pangenome to elucidate gene content in previously identified quantitative trait loci associated with adaptive traits. In one HDR, we found large deletions, spanning multiple genes, that are correlated with resistance to the anthelmintic drug abamectin. The C. elegans pangenome provides novel insights into genome and gene family evolution in a genetically diverse animal species, and empowers deeper investigations of genotype-phenotype relationships underlying adaptive traits, particularly in the context of structural and gene copy-number variation.

items.title: A near-infrared fluorescent genetically encoded calcium ion biosensor with a direct response
items.blurb: Near-infrared genetically encoded calcium ion (Ca2+) indicators (NIR GECIs) enable Ca2+ imaging at longer wavelengths than green or red fluorescent GECIs, providing reduced autofluorescence and phototoxicity, and improved compatibility with deep-tissue and multiplexed imaging applications. We have previously reported biliverdin (BV)-binding phytochrome-based NIR GECIs such as NIR-GECO2G that exhibit inverse fluorescence responses. Although inverse response GECIs can effectively report Ca2+ dynamics, their high baseline fluorescence in the resting apo state causes faster photobleaching and substantial out-of-focus background fluorescence, complicating signal interpretation. Here, using the inverse response NIR-GECO2G as the starting scaffold, we developed a direct response Ca2+ indicator, designated dNIR-GECO1.0, through iterative rounds of protein engineering and screening. dNIR-GECO1.0 exhibited greater molecular brightness than NIR-GECO2G, robust fluorescence in mammalian cells without exogenous BV supplementation, and a high dynamic range for reporting Ca2+ changes. A detailed mechanistic investigation identified the key mutations within the Ca2+ binding domain that were necessary to convert the inverse response indicator into a direct response indicator. Resonance Raman spectroscopic analysis provided insight into the specific changes in the BV chromophore resulting from the Ca2+-dependent conformational change.

items.title: Metabolic transitions reprogram translation through sequence-dependent regulation
items.blurb: Cells suppress protein synthesis during starvation, but how translation recovers upon nutrient repletion remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we followed translational recovery in budding yeast after repletion of glucose, nitrogen, or phosphate, combining time-resolved metabolomics, structural proteomics, transcriptomics, and spike-in-calibrated ribosome profiling. Nutrient addition rapidly altered ribosome occupancy in distinct, transcript-specific programs. To identify their sequence determinants, we developed RiboNet, a deep learning framework that predicts ribosome load and positions along transcripts from mRNA sequence. RiboNet-guided in silico mutagenesis revealed reduced pausing at serine codons upon glucose repletion and transiently increased pausing at leucine codons following nitrogen repletion. These responses coincided with altered cognate tRNA charging and metabolite-associated structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. RiboNet also identified a conserved 5' UTR motif, GAUY, that increased reporter protein output following glucose repletion. Our findings reveal how metabolic state alters the contributions of mRNA sequence features to translation initiation and elongation.

items.title: Native architecture of a mitochondrial oxphosome
items.blurb: Mitochondrial cristae are the primary bioenergetic units of eukaryotic cells, yet the molecular principles that dictate their morphologies remain largely unknown. Using in situ cryo-electron tomography and integrative modeling, we resolve the native organization of the respiratory machinery in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Unlike previously studied animals and green algae, diatoms possess tubular crista, a conserved membrane architecture found in diverse and globally relevant species. We identify several native supercomplexes assemblies, including an oxphosome comprising the entire respiratory chain. Our results, together with molecular dynamics analyses, reveal that these supercomplexes assemble through a lipid-mediated mechanism. We propose that tubular cristae are shaped by the interplay between membrane-bending ATP synthase oligomers that bud the hemispherical crista tips and supercomplexes that act as molecular roadblocks to constrain ATP synthase propagation, thereby balancing membrane curvature and allowing cristae body extension. Furthermore, we show that the diatom Complex I retains ancestral subunits related to fatty acid synthase. Beyond illuminating diatom bioenergetics, our findings reveal a fundamental principle of mitochondrial morphogenesis where ATP synthase-driven membrane curvature is spatially fine-tuned by respiratory supercomplexes.

items.title: LANCE-seq: Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction for Spatial Transcriptomics
items.blurb: Spatial transcriptomics enables the resolution of spatial heterogeneity in gene expression within tissues, yet most existing sequencing-based methods rely on ex vivo tissue processing, making it difficult to track dynamic molecular changes in the same living individual. We developed LANCE-seq (Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction sequencing), a live-tissue spatial transcriptomics platform based on encoded microneedle arrays that enables high-density spatial RNA capture through poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM) dendrimer-functionalized interfaces and microfluidic orthogonal combinatorial encoding. In frozen mouse brain tissue, LANCE-seq detected an average of 6,399 genes per spatial spot and reconstructed the spatial distribution of major brain regions and representative marker genes. Furthermore, in the acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver injury model, LANCE-seq enabled repeated sampling from the same living animal at different time points. At 6 h after APAP treatment, injury-related genes such as Hmox1, Ddit3, Atf3, and Fgf21 were significantly elevated, and transcriptional programs associated with stress, inflammation, and cellular injury were broadly enhanced. Meanwhile, liver zonation-related transcriptional signatures were remodeled, with different relative zonation states all exhibiting activation of injury programs. By integrating high-throughput spatial encoding with minimally invasive in vivo sampling, LANCE-seq provides a platform for longitudinal spatial transcriptomic studies of drug responses and disease progression.

items.title: PYTHOCHEMICAL COMPOSITION AND ANTIMICROBIAL ACTIVITY OF LEPIDIUM SATIVUM SEED EXTRACTS AGAINST SELECTED HUMAN PATHOGENS.
items.blurb: This study evaluates the antimicrobial activity of Lepidium sativum (Garden Cress) seed extracts against Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Fusarium oxysporum, and Candida albicans using methanol and acetone as solvents. The antimicrobial effects were assessed through the zone of inhibition and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) using serial dilution. The methanol extract exhibited the highest inhibition zones, measuring 23.6 mm for S. aureus and 21.5 mm for E. coli, while the acetone extract showed 22.9 mm and 18.3 mm, respectively. C. albicans exhibited moderate susceptibility, with inhibition zones of 16.2 mm (methanol) and 14.8 mm (acetone), whereas F. oxysporum showed weaker inhibition at 12.4 mm and 10.7 mm, respectively. MIC values ranged from 10-1 to 10-4 dilutions, with methanol extracts maintaining higher efficacy at lower concentrations. These findings validate Lepidium sativum as a potential natural antimicrobial agent, particularly against gram-positive bacteria, and suggest further exploration of its bioactive compounds for pharmaceutical applications.

items.title: Cumulative antibiograms: effects of isolate selection and stratification order on susceptibility estimates and resistance representation
items.blurb: Cumulative antibiograms depend on how isolates are selected and how data are stratified. Different selection strategies may affect both the number of isolates included and the susceptibility estimates reported. We retrospectively analyzed routine microbiology records from a tertiary-care hospital in Barcelona, Spain (2022-2025). Within each patient-organism-calendar-year unit, we compared three isolate-selection strategies: first-isolate, resistance-phenotype, and susceptibility-profile. We assessed the number of isolates retained, susceptibility at standard or increased exposure, the identification of resistance-phenotype profiles, and the effect of de-duplication before versus after stratification. Annual differences in susceptibility were estimated using paired cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptibility-profile selection retained 16.9% more isolates than first-isolate selection, with differences exceeding 5 percentage points in 10 of 44 annual antimicrobial comparisons. No annual susceptibility differences exceeding this threshold were observed for the other species. Resistance-phenotype and susceptibility-profile selection criteria identified 468 MDR and 278 XDR P. aeruginosa isolates. Of these, 90 (19.2%) of the MDR and 53 (19.1%) of the XDR isolates were not captured by first-isolate selection. In the broader stratification dataset, stratification-first processing increased first-isolate retention by 21.2% for blood specimens and 11.2% for inpatients. These findings show that modest changes in cumulative susceptibility can coexist with incomplete representation of resistant phenotypes. In conclusion, phenotype- and AST-profile-based selection capture additional resistance information beyond first-isolate selection, despite modest differences in cumulative susceptibility. Clinical validation is needed before their use to guide empirical therapy.

items.title: Region-Specific Changes in the Aging Enteric Nervous System
items.blurb: As human life expectancy increases, understanding the physiological changes that accompany aging becomes increasingly important. Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is common with age, and age-related changes in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which regulates GI motility, may contribute to this decline in function. Studies of the aging ENS have reported contradicting results, potentially reflecting the substantial regional heterogeneity of the ENS and the fact that most studies focus on only one or two areas of the GI tract. Neurons in the myenteric plexus, which regulate intestinal contractions and motility, are organized into ganglia that form circumferential stripes along the length of the gut. Here, we systematically compare neuronal and glial density and organization across all five regions of the small and large intestine in young (3-4 month-old) and aged (22-26 month-old) mice. We find that neuronal density remains unchanged with age across all regions, despite localized changes in ganglia organization. Although the overall stripe-like arrangement is preserved, ganglia are less aligned with stripes in the duodenum and ileum, while those in the ileum and distal colon are smaller, contain fewer neurons, and have a greater proportion of neurons located outside the ganglia. Glial cell numbers vary regionally with age, increasing in the duodenum and distal colon but decreasing in the proximal colon. The proportion of Calretinin+ neurons, meanwhile, remains stable across the small intestine. Together, these findings reveal that aging is associated with selective, region-specific remodeling of myenteric plexus cytoarchitecture rather than uniform structural decline across the GI tract. This comprehensive regional analysis may help reconcile conflicting reports of age-related changes in the ENS.

items.title: The global geometry of optimal neural representations
items.blurb: Efficient coding hypothesizes that neural activity optimally represents information under resource constraints. The global structures of such optimal population codes are difficult to study theoretically, and previous works have usually resorted to either focusing on local properties like fine discrimination or placing restrictions on the parametric forms of neural tuning. We address the general problem by analytically deriving the neural representation that minimizes the all-pairs average classification error of a one-dimensional circular variable under various forms of neural response noise. Our method is based on formulating the space of neural response distributions as a statistical manifold whose geometry can be simplified through a generalized version of variance-stabilizing transformations. The theory fully characterizes the complete family of optimal population codes and allows us to make two novel predictions. First, an optimal code should allow the existence of oppositely peaked bimodal tuning curves. Second, there should be a correlation between spike count variability and tuning sharpness. We validate both of these predictions in the mouse head direction system.

items.title: Energetic costs of osmo- and ionoregulatory responses to desiccation and recovery in a model insect
items.blurb: Climate change is expected to increase the frequency, duration and intensity of weather events that cause desiccation stress to small-bodied terrestrial insects. Whether a desiccation event may cause mortality depends on the time-dependent osmo- and ionoregulation responses of insects to desiccation and their recovery. Yet these responses and their associated energetic costs are not always clear for a range of mesic species. Here, we characterised the ability of house crickets (Acheta domesticus) to physiologically resist and recover from desiccation. We measured water loss from different tissues, changes in haemolymph volume and in haemolymph ion concentration as well as stored macromolecules (lipids, carbohydrates and proteins) use over a time-course of desiccation (0, 3, 6 or 18 h) and recovery with access to water and with or without access to food (18 h desiccation and 6 h recovery). During 18 h of desiccation, crickets regulated haemolymph ion concentration, avoiding hyperkalaemia and hypernatraemia, despite losing up to 14.5 and 21.1% of their body water for female and males respectively, across all body compartments. Recovery represented a distinct physiological phase to acute stress with a restoration of ion concentrations and body water with significant energetic contributions from stored macromolecules. We conclude crickets employ a general two-phase physiological strategy to withstand and recover from a short-term acute desiccation stress, establishing a physiological baseline to evaluate potential desiccation stress, and providing key insight into the time-dependency of osmoregulation and ion regulation for insects encountering fluctuating desiccation stress under climate change.

items.title: Myeloid mDIC Deficiency Remodels Adipose Macrophages to an Efferocytosis-Associated State and Improves Metabolic Homeostasis During Obesity
items.blurb: Obesity-associated adipose inflammation contributes to metabolic dysfunction, yet the mechanisms linking mitochondrial metabolism to macrophage efferocytosis remain incompletely understood. The mitochondrial dicarboxylate carrier (mDIC), encoded by SLC25A10, regulates adipocyte function, but its role in macrophages remains unclear. Here, we investigated how myeloid mDIC deficiency affects mitochondrial function, macrophage heterogeneity, and metabolic homeostasis during diet-induced obesity. We observed reduced mDIC protein expression in subcutaneous white adipose tissue from individuals with obesity, whereas palmitate increased mDIC expression in mouse and human macrophages. Myeloid mDIC deletion preserved mitochondrial respiration under palmitate stress. Single-cell RNA sequencing of adipose stromal vascular cells from high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice revealed an expanded efferocytosis-associated macrophage population and reduced proportions of inflammatory and lipid-associated macrophages. Consistently, mDIC-deficient macrophages exhibited increased Mertk expression and greater association with apoptotic cells. Pharmacological inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase or electron transport markedly suppressed apoptotic cell uptake, including the quenching-resistant fraction, without substantially affecting macrophage viability. In vivo, myeloid mDIC deletion attenuated HFD-induced weight gain, improved insulin sensitivity, and increased CD11c-CD206 adipose macrophage abundance, accompanied by elevated expression of alternative activation-associated markers. Together, these findings identify myeloid mDIC as an important regulator of macrophage mitochondrial function and adipose immune remodeling during obesity, suggesting a novel mechanism by which mitochondrial bioenergetics contribute to macrophage apoptotic-cell handling and metabolic homeostasis.

items.title: World: Ending violence against children: From commitment to reality
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Violence against children remains one of the most widespread violations of children’s rights worldwide. Despite global commitments to end all forms of violence against children, millions of children continue to experience violence across regions and income levels, revealing the persistent gap between commitment and reality.

This brief presents the latest available global estimates on violent discipline by caregivers in the home and sexual violence in childhood, drawing on evidence from both development and humanitarian contexts. The brief illustrates why accelerating progress towards SDG Target 16.2 remains an urgent priority and highlights the essential role of both universal and targeted prevention efforts and a strong, accessible social service workforce equipped with a package of evidence-based family support and child protection services.

Accelerating progress will require renewed political commitment, sustained investment, stronger child protection systems capable of delivering evidence-based services at scale in cooperation with allied services such as health, education, and justice, and the large-scale implementation of proven universal and targeted prevention interventions.

items.title: World: A record high of nearly one in four children now live in conflict zones - Save the Children report
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

· Nearly one in four children worldwide live in conflict zones, new report finds

· Africa now accounts for 44% of children living near conflict worldwide, with an unprecedented two in five African children impacted

· Verified incidents of denial of humanitarian access against children have increased almost 16-fold in a decade to almost one an hour

AMMAN, 19 November 2026 – Almost one in four children worldwide are now living in conflict zones, the highest number since records began in 1990, according to a new Save the Children report.

The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025, according to the report Stop the War on Children: Changing the Odds, which draws on data from the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO).

The report found that the share of the world’s children living in conflict zones more than doubled from about 10% in the mid-1990s to 23.4% in 2025.

Africa is home to the highest number of children living in conflict zones, accounting for about 260 million, or 44% of the global total. This is nearly a 20% increase from the 218 million children in Africa who lived in conflict zones in 2024.

Across Africa, the proportion of children living in conflict zones more than tripled from about one in eight children in 2010 to about two in five in 2025, the highest level ever recorded for the continent. This puts Africa on par with the Middle East, where both regions now have two in five children living in conflict zones.

Elsewhere, about one in four children (24.2%) in the Americas lived in conflict zones in 2025, one in seven (14.3%) in Asia, and nearly one in nine (10.6%) in Europe.

The report also examined United Nations verified grave violations against children in armed conflict between 2005 and 2025, including killing and maiming, recruitment by armed forces or groups, sexual violence, abduction, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access. These numbers represent the tip of the iceberg for grave violations against children, as most attacks on children go unverified, said Save the Children.

Killing and maiming accounted for the largest share of violations against children over the past two decades, with 171,712 cases verified since 2005. More than 70% of the cases were committed against children in five countries: the occupied Palestinian territory, Afghanistan, Somalia, Syria and Yemen.

The report also found that the fastest-growing grave violation against children is the denial of humanitarian aid, with verified incidents skyrocketing from 509 in 2015 to 8,322 in 2025, more than a 16-fold increase in a decade. This amounts to almost one verified incident of denial of humanitarian aid every hour, on average, in 2025. More than 70% of all verified aid denial last year took place against Palestinian children.

Denial of humanitarian access rose from just over 2% of all verified grave violations in 2015 to more than 21% in 2025, making it the second most frequently verified violation after killing and maiming.

Rape and other forms of sexual violence against children are widely underreported. Even so, the report found that 28,909 cases have been verified since reporting began. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) accounts for 12,698, or almost 44% of the total, followed by Somalia with 4,534 and Chad with 2,979. Together, the three countries account for around 70% of all verified cases.

In eastern DRC, 17-year-old Ana* experienced the devastating consequences of conflict after violence forced her family from their home. After months of displacement, they returned, only for armed men to break into their house, shoot Ana’s brother dead and rape her while other family members were assaulted.

“We had fled the war, but it came knocking at our door again. [When the attackers came to our home] I screamed; I begged for mercy… but no one listened. My brother was killed before my eyes. I was raped,” Ana said. “[Afterwards] the hardest part wasn’t the pain. It was people’s mockery. They pointed fingers at me, as if I were to blame for what had been done to me.”

The next morning, neighbours helped Ana reach a local health centre supported by Save the Children, where she received emergency medical care, including treatment to prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, as well as ongoing psychosocial support.

Gudrun Østby, Research Professor at PRIO, said: “We estimate that 589 million children were living close to armed conflict last year. These record-high figures are a stark reminder that conflict is devastating the daily lives, education, health and future prospects of hundreds of millions of children. Unless greater efforts are made to protect children in conflict settings, the consequences of today's wars will be felt for decades to come.”

Inger Ashing, CEO of Save the Children International, said:

“Almost one in four children around the world now lives in a conflict zone. What could be more important than their protection? The scale of this crisis is rapidly growing, and the systems meant to protect children are being pushed to breaking point.

“We're seeing aid weaponised, attacked and deliberately disrupted. Humanitarian organisations are denied access, funding is being slashed, and needs are outpacing our ability to reach every child in crisis. Meanwhile, parties to conflict continue to disregard the rules of war, while new military technologies are changing how wars are fought, increasing the risk further for children in conflict settings.

“Children’s rights and needs must be at the centre of decisions about war, peace and security. More than 20 years of monitoring violations have made the horrors children face visible and created opportunities to prevent further harm. This work must be protected, supported and translated into action.

"Parties to conflict must uphold the rules of war, and those responsible for violations must be held to account. But ensuring the protection of children isn’t only the responsibility of those fighting. States, donors and companies with leverage over perpetrators must use it, through diplomatic and political pressure. To truly change the odds for children living in conflict zones, we must put their protection first and work towards the peace they deserve.”

Save the Children is calling on parties to the conflict to uphold international humanitarian law, accounting for children’ distinct vulnerabilities, and to facilitate safe and unimpeded humanitarian relief to civilians. It is also urging governments to strengthen accountability for violations against children, implement international treaties and declarations that protect children and education in war zones, address the root causes of conflict and ensure children’s voices are heard in decisions affecting their futures.

In 2025, Save the Children worked in 107 countries, reaching more than 58.2 million people, including 37.8 million children. The child rights organisation also responded to 113 humanitarian crises in 63 countries, supporting over 24 million people, including 13.6 million children.

ENDS

Notes to Editor:

Read the full report here: https://resourcecentre.savethechildren.net/document/stop-the-war-on-children-changing-the-odds-2026

· The updated analysis on the number and share of children living in conflict zones is conducted by the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). The core dataset used to map conflict patterns in this report is the Uppsala Conflict Data Program’s Georeferenced Event Data Set (UCDP GED) until 2025. To estimate the number of children living in conflict areas, and populations more generally, PRIO integrated the UCDP conflict data with population data from CIESIN’s Gridded Population of the World (GPW) and from the UN World Population Prospects. PRIO uses UCDP’s definition of armed conflict: ‘armed force used by an organized actor against another organized actor, or against civilians, resulting in at least 25 battle-related deaths in one calendar year’. A ‘conflict zone’ is defined as an area within 50km of where one or more conflict incidents take place in a given year, within the borders of a country.

· The UN Security Council has identified six grave violations against children in situations of armed conflict: killing and maiming of children; recruitment or use of children by armed forces and groups; sexual violence against children; abduction of children; attacks against schools and hospitals; and denial of humanitarian access for children. These grave violations were defined on the basis of their egregious nature and their severe impact on children’s wellbeing.

Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

SAN SALVADOR – Los siete países que integran el Marco Integral Regional para la Protección y Soluciones (MIRPS) –Belice, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, México y Panamá– concluyeron hoy la IX Reunión Anual del MIRPS con la adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II, mediante la cual renovaron sus compromisos para fortalecer los sistemas nacionales de protección, ampliar las oportunidades de inclusión socioeconómica y avanzar en soluciones duraderas para personas con necesidades de protección y las comunidades que las acogen.

Durante el encuentro, celebrado bajo el liderazgo del Gobierno de El Salvador en su calidad de Presidencia Pro-Témpore 2026, autoridades de los países MIRPS, representantes de la Plataforma de Apoyo y socios estratégicos realizaron un balance de los avances alcanzados durante 2026 y examinaron las oportunidades y las prioridades que orientarán la cooperación regional en 2027. El diálogo destacó los resultados y buenas prácticas en materia de asilo, protección a nivel territorial, gobernabilidad local y medios de vida.

La Reunión Anual culminó con la adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II, en la que los Estados acordaron promover procedimientos de asilo más accesibles, eficientes y de calidad, ampliar el acceso a empleo, educación y medios de vida, e incorporar enfoques de protección en las políticas de gestión del riesgo de desastres y adaptación al cambio climático.

Los países también destacaron la importancia de profundizar la cooperación con otros mecanismos regionales y fortalecer las alianzas con gobiernos locales, sociedad civil, organizaciones lideradas por personas refugiadas, academia, sector privado y actores del desarrollo, con el propósito de ampliar el alcance y la sostenibilidad de las respuestas. Asimismo, reconocieron el valor del MIRPS como una plataforma regional que permite promover respuestas coordinadas en beneficio de las personas con necesidades de protección y las comunidades de acogida.

La Organización de los Estados Americanos (OEA), que integra junto con ACNUR la Secretaría Técnica del MIRPS, destacó los avances del Fondo MIRPS, cuyos proyectos han beneficiado a más de 33.000 personas en la región, y agradeció las contribuciones de España, la República de Corea y Portugal. “El desplazamiento sigue afectando a personas y familias en todo nuestro hemisferio. Atender sus necesidades va más allá de brindar protección inmediata y requiere instituciones sólidas, políticas inclusivas y una cooperación regional que abra caminos hacia la estabilidad y las oportunidades. Estos principios guían la Agenda de Paz y Prosperidad para las Américas de la OEA. En nuestro trabajo con las personas desplazadas, esto significa acceso a la protección, la documentación, la educación y el empleo, así como oportunidades para desarrollar su autonomía y vivir con dignidad”, afirmó Albert R. Ramdin, Secretario General de la OEA, al destacar el compromiso de la Organización con la protección y la inclusión de las personas con necesidades de protección.

En el marco del 75.º aniversario de la Convención sobre el Estatuto de los Refugiados de 1951, ACNUR destacó la importancia de mantener el compromiso regional con la protección internacional. “La adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II demuestra que los países de la región siguen apostando por la cooperación, la solidaridad y la responsabilidad compartida para responder al desplazamiento. A través del MIRPS, los Estados continúan transformando sus compromisos en acciones concretas para las personas refugiadas, desplazadas y las comunidades que las acogen", afirmó Isabel Márquez, Directora Regional de ACNUR para las Américas.

Los miembros de la Plataforma de Apoyo al MIRPS reafirmaron su compromiso de continuar acompañando los esfuerzos de los países mediante la cooperación técnica, la movilización de recursos y el fortalecimiento de alianzas estratégicas para apoyar la implementación de las prioridades nacionales y regionales, ampliar las oportunidades de protección y soluciones duraderas, y contribuir a la sostenibilidad de los esfuerzos impulsados por los Estados que integran este Mecanismo.

Al cierre de la IX Reunión Anual, El Salvador traspasó la Presidencia Pro-Témpore del MIRPS a Guatemala, que liderará el mecanismo durante 2027, en un año particularmente significativo en el que el MIRPS conmemorará su décimo aniversario.

A una década de la adopción de la Declaración de San Pedro Sula, este Mecanismo continúa consolidándose como una plataforma regional de cooperación, innovación y responsabilidad compartida que permite a los Estados avanzar conjuntamente en la protección, la inclusión y las soluciones para las personas refugiadas, desplazadas y otras personas con necesidades de protección internacional.

El Marco Integral Regional para la Protección y Soluciones (MIRPS) está integrado por Belice, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, México y Panamá. Es un mecanismo regional para la aplicación del Pacto Mundial sobre los Refugiados que promueve la cooperación y la responsabilidad compartida en materia de prevención, protección y soluciones duraderas frente al desplazamiento. La Plataforma de Apoyo al MIRPS, creada en 2019, contribuye a movilizar recursos y cooperación internacional. ACNUR y la OEA, a través de su Departamento de Acceso a Derechos (DAR), integran la Secretaría Técnica del MIRPS y su Plataforma de Apoyo.

items.title: Bangladesh: Estudios de ACNUR y la Universidad de Oxford advierten que el recorte de fondos aumenta el riesgo de que los refugiados sean víctimas de trata y explotación infantil
items.blurb:
Countries: Bangladesh, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Myanmar, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan
Sources: UN High Commissioner for Refugees, University of Oxford

GINEBRA/OXFORD – Los recortes cada vez más profundos en la financiación están aumentando el riesgo de que las personas refugiadas – especialmente las niñas y los niños – sean víctimas de trata, explotación o abuso, a medida que se van debilitando los sistemas de protección que garantizan su seguridad, de acuerdo con dos nuevos estudios presentados hoy por ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, y el Nuffield College de la Universidad de Oxford.

Los informes se centran en dos importantes países que acogen refugiados, Bangladés y Etiopía, cada uno de los cuales acoge a más de un millón de personas refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo. En ambos casos, los estudios han encontrado pruebas de que, cuando se recortan simultáneamente los servicios de protección y la asistencia esencial – como el alojamiento y la educación –, se debilitan las salvaguardias fundamentales y la población refugiada, que ya se encuentra en situación de vulnerabilidad, se enfrenta a riesgos cada vez mayores de explotación, trabajo peligroso y trata.

“Estos estudios destacan una realidad crítica y a menudo pasada por alto: los servicios de protección, como la asistencia jurídica, los espacios seguros, el apoyo psicosocial, la prevención de la violencia de género y la protección de las niñas y los niños, se encuentran entre las salvaguardias más sólidas contra la trata y la explotación”, afirmó Elizabeth Tan, Directora de Protección Internacional y Soluciones de ACNUR. “Cuando se recortan, las vulnerabilidades se agravan y a los traficantes les resulta más fácil aprovecharse de personas que ya se encuentran en situación de riesgo. Invertir en protección ahora previene la explotación futura”.

En Bangladés, los casos de trata detectados en el mayor asentamiento de refugiados del mundo, cerca de Cox’s Bazar, aumentaron un 28 por ciento entre 2024 y 2025. Las niñas y los niños representaron el 17 por ciento de las víctimas detectadas en 2025, frente al 14 por ciento en 2024. Entre enero y septiembre de 2026, se identificaron 411 víctimas de la trata, de las cuales casi el 23 por ciento eran niñas y niños, lo que subraya los crecientes riesgos en materia de protección a los que se enfrentan las personas refugiadas rohingyas.

Estos riesgos se agravan a medida que los recursos humanitarios se reducen mientras que las necesidades aumentan. Entre 2024 y 2025, la población refugiada rohingya en Bangladés aumentó en torno al 17 por ciento, lo que supone más de 170.000 refugiados, mientras que el presupuesto operativo de ACNUR se redujo en más del 8 por ciento en 2025 y se enfrentó a un déficit de financiación del 59 por ciento en comparación con las necesidades totales. Alrededor del 88 por ciento de los hogares rohingyas informaron de un deterioro del estado de sus alojamientos, y a casi ninguno de los refugiados recién llegados se le pudo asignar un alojamiento propio. La disponibilidad de agua potable descendió de 33 litros por persona y día en 2024 a 23 litros en 2025, situación agravada en parte por la prolongada sequía en la zona, con un promedio de 21 personas compartiendo cada letrina.

Debido a las restricciones de la libertad de movimiento y de empleo, las personas refugiadas rohingyas – la gran mayoría de las cuales son además apátridas – siguen dependiendo en gran medida de la asistencia humanitaria, y el 35 por ciento de los hogares dependía por completo de la ayuda en 2025. A medida que la asistencia y los servicios esenciales se ven sometidos a una gran presión y los recortes de financiación afectan a todos los actores humanitarios sobre el terreno, las personas refugiadas se ven expuestas a mayores riesgos de trata, trabajo forzado, matrimonio forzado, trabajo infantil y peligrosos viajes marítimos en busca de protección y dignidad.

En Etiopía, los recortes presupuestarios han reducido significativamente los servicios de protección para las niñas y los niños refugiados, que representan el 52 por ciento de la población refugiada del país – procedentes principalmente de Sudán del Sur, Somalia, Eritrea y Sudán –, entre los que se incluyen al menos 31.000 menores no acompañados y separados de sus familias. En 2025, la operación de ACNUR en Etiopía contó con menos de un tercio de la financiación prevista, mientras que solo se cubrió el 18 por ciento de las necesidades previstas en materia de protección infantil durante el año.

Los recortes presupuestarios están debilitando la red de agentes de protección, las estructuras comunitarias y las vías de derivación que contribuyen a que los niños refugiados sigan siendo visibles y estén a salvo. Seis socios de protección de ACNUR en Etiopía se vieron obligados a reducir su plantilla en casi la mitad. Entre 2024 y 2025, el apoyo de ACNUR a la localización de familiares y a la reunificación familiar de los niños en Etiopía separados de sus padres y cuidadores se redujo en más de la mitad, pasando de 4.071 a 1.887 niños atendidos. Tanto la atención alternativa para menores no acompañados como los programas de fortalecimiento familiar se redujeron en aproximadamente la mitad, y el número de niñas y niños refugiados sujetos a procedimientos de ‘interés superior’ – destinados a garantizar que las decisiones que les afectan den prioridad a su seguridad, bienestar y derechos – se redujo en un tercio. La falta de financiación también afectó a 57 escuelas primarias que atienden a alrededor de 110.000 niñas y niños refugiados, mientras que el apoyo psicosocial se redujo en un 29 por ciento.

En este sombrío contexto de financiación, observaciones recientes sobre el terreno apuntan a un preocupante aumento del trabajo infantil entre los refugiados, incluido el trabajo en la agricultura y el desplazamiento hacia zonas mineras informales. Junto con la reducción de los servicios, estas tendencias dejan a niñas y niños refugiados – ya de por sí vulnerables, especialmente a aquellos que huyeron solos, se vieron separados de sus familias o a las niñas refugiadas – más expuestos a la explotación, la violencia sexual, el matrimonio infantil y la trata con fines de trabajo forzado y explotación sexual, al tiempo que reducen las oportunidades de identificar y responder a los riesgos.

“Estos casos de estudio ilustran lo que se puede lograr cuando se establece un vínculo eficaz entre los ámbitos de la investigación, las políticas y la práctica. El Nuffield College se enorgullece de haber colaborado con ACNUR para crear algo que ninguna de las dos partes habría podido lograr por sí sola”, afirmó el profesor Andrew Thompson, del Nuffield College de la Universidad de Oxford. “Los resultados dan mucho que pensar y constituyen una severa advertencia a la comunidad internacional sobre lo que podría suceder si los servicios esenciales de prevención y protección para las personas refugiadas siguen sin contar con los recursos suficientes”.

Aunque ACNUR y sus socios siguen estableciendo prioridades, adaptándose e innovando bajo graves restricciones financieras, ambos estudios concluyen que una financiación sostenida, flexible y predecible sigue siendo esencial para garantizar la protección de los refugiados. Sin embargo, la situación sigue siendo grave en 2026: los programas globales de ACNUR para la protección de la niñez solo cuentan con un 25 por ciento de financiación, y las iniciativas para prevenir y responder a la violencia de género, con apenas un 24 por ciento hasta julio de 2026.

Los estudios refuerzan el llamado a la acción urgente y destacan que la inversión en la protección de las personas refugiadas y de la niñez, así como en el fortalecimiento de los sistemas nacionales, no solo es un imperativo humanitario y de protección, sino también una inversión rentable en prevención, resiliencia y soluciones.

items.title: Atrocity Alert No. 503: Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Ethiopia and Afghanistan
items.blurb:
Countries: occupied Palestinian territory, Afghanistan, Eritrea, Ethiopia
Source: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect

Atrocity Alert is a weekly publication by the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect highlighting situations where populations are at risk of, or are enduring, mass atrocity crimes.

WINTER FLOODING BEGINS IN GAZA AMID DEVASTATION WROUGHT BY ISRAEL

As Palestinians brace for the fourth winter since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, living conditions across the enclave are becoming more dire amid the onset of seasonal flooding. The first major winter storm of the season, on 6 November, resulted in the flooding of over 700,000 tents housing displaced persons in a single day. Thousands of families were left without shelter, essential services were disrupted and in the days that followed several people were killed when a sand dune collapsed onto their tent.

Noting the continued constraints to distributing essential aid ahead of winter, UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher has called for immediate action to end the “collective punishment” and “predictable, preventable suffering” of Palestinians in Gaza. He stressed that humanitarians had sounded the alarm for months about the need for essential winter supplies, only to be told by foreign ministers and other partners to wait for progress following Israeli elections in October.

Israel’s conduct across the enclave places Palestinians in Gaza at particular risk during winter. Over 80 percent of all structures remain damaged or destroyed, while Israel continues to deny entry of major reconstruction materials, further undermining water and sanitation, healthcare facilities, energy supplies and housing. Of the approximately 1.7 million people who remain internally displaced, some 1.4 million are living in tents or makeshift shelters, with roughly 950,000 confined to flood-prone areas, according to the World Health Organization. More than a year after the so-called ceasefire took effect, Palestinians remain unable to rebuild critical, life-sustaining infrastructure and lack even adequate temporary shelter. Israel continues to obstruct the delivery of tents, with over 150,000 awaiting entry approval just outside Gaza.

The consequences of these conditions are already evident. An infant has died from severe hypothermia, acute respiratory infections have increased by 33,000 cases compared to the same period last year and hospitals in Gaza have reported a surge in meningitis cases among children. On 12 November a joint media stakeout at the UN, led by the United Kingdom, Qatar and Jordan and involving 53 countries and international organizations, called for urgent humanitarian access to Gaza as winter nears. Earlier in the day, an Israeli airstrike hit a hospital in Gaza, killing six people and injuring 27 others.

Israel must immediately open all border crossings for Gaza, allow unimpeded access for humanitarian aid and ensure humanitarian organizations can operate freely across the enclave. States must enact concrete measures to ensure Israel upholds its obligations under international law and its responsibilities as an occupying power toward Palestinians in Gaza, including by halting arms transfers to Israel, suspending trade agreements and imposing targeted sanctions on Israeli officials.

ETHIOPIA–ERITREA BORDER CLASHES HEIGHTEN RISKS OF FURTHER ATROCITIES

Reports of clashes between Ethiopian and Eritrean forces near the long-disputed border town of Badme have heightened fears of a wider regional conflict. Between 11 and 13 November the Ethiopian National Defense Forces and Eritrean Defense Forces reportedly exchanged fire, with Ethiopian drones and Eritrean heavy artillery deployed near the border.

Badme was at the center of the devastating 1998–2000 Ethiopia-Eritrea war, which ended with the signing of the Algiers Peace Agreement in December 2000. In 2002 the independent Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission awarded Badme to Eritrea. However, Ethiopia’s refusal to implement the ruling contributed to nearly two decades of hostility between the two countries. While engagement between Ethiopia and Eritrea improved significantly following a historic rapprochement in 2018 and the countries subsequently allied during the 2020–2022 war in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, relations have since deteriorated. Notably, over the past year, tensions have mounted as the two countries have publicly exchanged statements over Ethiopia’s aspirations to secure access to a port on the Red Sea. Diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea broke down in September amid renewed fighting in Tigray.

Amid growing regional tensions, atrocity risks are also mounting within Ethiopia. In Oromia, at least 94 Orthodox Christians were reportedly killed in a series of attacks between 20 October and 5 November. The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission attributed a 24 October attack in Sirka district to the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), documenting civilian deaths and attacks on civilian infrastructure. The OLA has rejected this finding. Attacks targeting civilians on the basis of their ethnicity may constitute the crime against humanity of persecution if committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population.

Violence has also escalated around Moyale since October, where clashes involving forces and militias affiliated with the Oromia and Somali regional authorities have fueled longstanding disputes over administrative boundaries, territory and resources. The violence has displaced an estimated 50,000 people into neighboring Kenya, with women and children arriving in urgent need of food, shelter and medical assistance.

Ethiopia and Eritrea must cease hostilities, resume diplomatic dialogue and protect civilians. Ethiopian authorities must safeguard vulnerable communities, investigate attacks and pursue a peaceful resolution to the Oromia-Somali border dispute. The Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect’s Horn of Africa expert, Sarah Hunter, said, “Escalating tensions across Ethiopia and its borders threaten to engulf the Horn of Africa. Without urgent action to address these interconnected crises, civilians face a growing risk of further atrocities. The international community, including the UN and African Union, must prioritize diplomacy and accountability to ensure a durable peace.”

CLOSURE OF AFGHANISTAN ICC CASE LEAVES ACCOUNTABILITY GAPS

On 12 November the International Criminal Court (ICC) Pre-Trial Chamber II ordered the formal closure of the Situation in Afghanistan I case, finding that the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) failed to “effectively carry out any further investigative or prosecutorial activities.” Authorized in 2020, the investigation covered alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed on Afghan territory from 1 May 2003 involving United States (US) military and intelligence actors, former Afghan government forces and the Taliban, as well as the so-called Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant-Khorasan. Alleged crimes included murder, torture, deliberate attacks against civilians and unlawful detention. On 13 November the OTP filed a notice of appeal and requested a stay of the closure decision.

The decision follows a series of procedural disputes over the scope and organization of the Afghanistan investigation. In 2026 the Chamber separated the proceedings into two situations: Afghanistan II, concerning alleged crimes committed by the Taliban since the 2021 takeover, and Afghanistan I, covering the remaining aspects of the original investigation. Closing Afghanistan I consequently leaves a significant accountability gap for atrocity crimes committed by a range of actors across more than two decades of conflict.

The closure comes amid a drastic escalation in US pressure on the Court. On 9 October the US imposed institution-wide sanctions on the ICC, marking a drastic escalation in its campaign against the Court and threatening its ability to pursue accountability for the world’s gravest crimes. The US has repeatedly sought to obstruct the Court’s work, including to prevent potential prosecutions of US nationals. While the sanctions and the closure decision are distinct developments, the decision risks further narrowing the Court’s pursuit of accountability for alleged crimes involving US personnel.

While the ICC unsealed on 5 October four arrest warrants in the Afghanistan II situation against senior Taliban officials for the alleged crime against humanity of gender persecution, the closure of Afghanistan I underscores the importance of other initiatives to contribute to accountability, most notably the UN Human Rights Council-mandated Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan (IIM-A). The IIM-A is the only international investigative body mandated to collect, preserve and analyze evidence of serious violations and abuses perpetrated by all parties in Afghanistan, which may support future accountability efforts. The IIM-A’s mandate is not time-limited, meaning it can assess past, ongoing and future crimes.

The international community must ensure that the closure of one accountability pathway does not end efforts to secure justice for victims and survivors. State parties to the Rome Statute should stand firmly with the victims of atrocity crimes and support the OTP’s appeal and request for a stay of the closure decision pending the Appeals Chamber’s determination. UN member states must ensure the IIM-A is fully operationalized without delay and provided with the political, financial and technical support its mandate demands.

items.title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Kenya | Nigeria Weekly External Situation Report 27, Data as of 15 November 2026
items.blurb:
Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Nigeria
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues at a high and sustained level of transmission. During epidemiological week 46 (9 – 15 November 2026), 442 confirmed cases and 239 confirmed deaths were reported, compared with 458 cases and 228 deaths in week 45; the national seven-day average has remained between 62 and 65 cases per day, and a new health zone, Watsa in Haut-Uélé, reported its first confirmed cases. Over three epidemiological weeks (weeks 44 – 46 compared with weeks 41 – 43), reported cases decreased by 6.7% and deaths by 4.6%, with a decline in Ituri partly offset by continued intense transmission in Nord-Kivu, where Beni remains the health zone with the most cases, and by rising incidence in Mangala, Mambasa and Mutwanga. Deaths in treatment centres increased in week 46 and the proportion of deaths occurring in the community fell to 59% (142 of 239), its lowest weekly level since August. In Kenya, the last patient was discharged on 11 November, and all contacts have completed their follow-up; the 42-day countdown is under way, and the event has not yet been declared over. In Nigeria, all 62 contacts completed their 21-day follow-up on 13 November and no secondary case was identified; surveillance continues in both countries. Additionally, Nigeria started the 42 days countdown on 27 Oct after the case was medically evacuated to Switzerland on the 26 October 2026.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, insecurity in Beni, Mabalako and Bafwasende, strikes over unpaid salaries in several provinces and community resistance to safe burials continue to constrain surveillance and response operations.

items.title: Venezuela: Nuevas rutas migratorias cobran fuerza en América del Sur mientras los cruces por el Darién caen un 90 %, según la OIM
items.blurb:
Countries: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Haiti, Honduras, Panama, Uruguay, World
Source: International Organization for Migration

Ciudad de Panamá, 18 de noviembre de 2026 – La migración en América Latina y el Caribe está experimentando una transformación marcada por la consolidación de nuevas rutas migratorias en América del Sur y una disminución del 90 % en los cruces hacia el norte a través del Darién, en Panamá, en comparación con el primer semestre de 2025, según un nuevo informe de la Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM).

«La marcada disminución de los cruces por el Darién es solo una parte de la realidad. La migración no se ha detenido. Las personas están encontrando nuevas rutas, desplazándose en distintas direcciones y tomando decisiones difíciles sobre dónde construir su futuro», afirmó Juan Francisco Espinosa, Director Regional de la OIM para las Américas. «Debemos adaptarnos a estos cambios para garantizar que se protejan los derechos de las personas migrantes durante sus desplazamientos».

Por primera vez, la OIM identifica la ruta del este de América del Sur como un corredor migratorio plenamente consolidado, que se extiende desde el Caribe, a través del norte de América del Sur, hasta el Brasil y el Cono Sur. Mientras disminuye el número de personas que se desplazan hacia el norte por Centroamérica, otras viajan hacia el sur, retornan a sus países de origen o se establecen en países como Brasil y Uruguay. La disminución de los movimientos tradicionales hacia el norte no significa necesariamente que haya menos personas en movimiento, sino que los patrones migratorios en la región están cambiando.

Durante los primeros cuatro meses de 2026, aproximadamente 3.000 personas cubanas ingresaron al Brasil cada mes, mientras que, en el Uruguay, se registró un saldo migratorio positivo de 5.946 personas cubanas entre enero y mayo. En conjunto, estas tendencias sugieren que América del Sur se está convirtiendo en un destino cada vez más importante para las personas migrantes, en lugar de ser únicamente una región de tránsito. La respuesta de los países, incluido el acceso a una situación migratoria regular y al empleo, determinará en gran medida las oportunidades de estas personas para contribuir a las comunidades de acogida.

La ruta recientemente identificada se suma a la ruta centroamericana y la ruta andina como uno de los tres principales corredores migratorios que configuran los movimientos en América Latina y el Caribe. Las tres rutas están experimentando cambios significativos, con personas migrantes que se desplazan cada vez más en distintas direcciones, permanecen temporalmente en otros países o deciden establecerse en nuevos destinos.

También está aumentando el número de personas migrantes que regresan a sus países de origen, aunque estas dinámicas distan de ser sencillas. Entre las personas venezolanas que viajaban hacia el sur por Guatemala, el 74 % indicó que tenía intención de retornar a la República Bolivariana de Venezuela. Otras tenían previsto continuar hacia Honduras, Colombia o Costa Rica.

A lo largo de la ruta andina, los movimientos registrados en el Ecuador se distribuyeron de forma relativamente equilibrada: el 55 % se dirigía hacia el norte y el 45 % hacia el sur. Esto refleja patrones migratorios cada vez más complejos, en los que las personas se desplazan entre países, regresan a destinos anteriores o continúan sus trayectos hacia otros lugares.

Mientras tanto, la disminución de los movimientos por las rutas tradicionales hacia el norte se extiende más allá de Panamá. Los movimientos hacia el norte por Honduras disminuyeron un 75 % en comparación con el primer semestre de 2025, lo que refuerza la evidencia de un cambio significativo en los patrones migratorios de Centroamérica.

«Estos cambios reflejan la evolución de los entornos normativos, las modificaciones en el acceso a vías migratorias regulares y las presiones económicas en toda la región», añadió Espinosa. «Las personas migrantes están tomando nuevas rutas, retornando a sus hogares o buscando oportunidades en otros lugares. Algunas quedan varadas durante el trayecto. Ante la evolución de los movimientos migratorios tanto regulares como irregulares, debemos trabajar con los gobiernos para ampliar las vías migratorias seguras y regulares y reducir los riesgos a los que se enfrentan las personas».

El informe destaca la importancia de dar seguimiento a estos cambios a medida que se producen. A través de su Matriz de Seguimiento de los Desplazamientos (DTM, por sus siglas en inglés), la OIM recopila y analiza datos sobre los movimientos migratorios, lo que permite a los gobiernos y a los socios humanitarios comprender mejor las rutas emergentes, identificar las necesidades de las personas y planificar respuestas adecuadas.

Esta información fundamentada en datos permite a los gobiernos gestionar los cambios en los movimientos migratorios de manera ordenada y previsible, al tiempo que brinda apoyo tanto a las personas migrantes como a las comunidades de acogida.
